title: No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Buist I, Bredeweg SW, van Mechelen W, Lemmink KA, Pepping GJ, Diercks RL
population: Novice runners preparing for a 4-mile (6.7 km) recreational event (GRONORUN trial)
findings: Two-arm RCT compared a standard 8-week training program with an adapted, graded 13-week program based on the 10% training rule.
RRI incidence was 20.8% in the graded group and 20.3% in the standard group (chi2 = 0.016, df = 1, P = .90): the graded program was not preventive.
RRI was defined as any musculoskeletal complaint of the lower extremity or back restricting running for at least 1 week; both groups recorded running and injury in an internet-based log.
532 novice runners were randomised to a graded 13-week program based on the 10% training rule or a standard 8-week program.
RRI incidence was 20.8% in the graded group and 20.3% in the standard group (chi-squared = 0.016, df = 1, P = .90).
RRI was defined as any musculoskeletal complaint of the lower extremity or back causing a restriction of running for at least 1 week.
The authors concluded the 10%-rule graded program had no effect on RRI incidence compared with the standard 8-week program.
limitations: Novice runners only and a short event-preparation program. The two arms differed in length (13 vs 8 weeks) as well as progression, and the graded arm used a program built on the 10% rule rather than verified strict adherence. Not generalisable to experienced runners or long-distance training.
implications: The 10% weekly rule has no RCT support as an injury preventive; do not present it as a safety guarantee or hard constraint on weekly volume.
Keep weekly progression a soft default and let the session-spike rule (Frandsen 2025) act as the actual guard.
User-facing copy must not claim that following the 10% rule prevents injury.
Do not claim the 10% weekly-increase rule prevents injuries in novices; use it as a default convention and rely on other levers (exposure caps, rest weeks, strength work).
No change to the 10% default is justified by this trial alone, and the rule should not be applied rigidly at very low volumes where 10% is a trivial change (an engineering judgement, not a finding).
